before.title: LEGO Hubble Space Telescope (11382): Worth ₹18,200?
before.content:
Your wallet just got a cosmic call, and it’s not a friendly one. The LEGO Hubble Space Telescope ([11382](/sets/11382-hubble-space-telescope)) is priced at an estimated ₹18,200, which will make any EMI calculator blush. This minifigure‑scale homage to the iconic telescope lands with 1,252 pieces, a respectable count for a display‑oriented build in the Icons line.

First impressions matter, and the box art does a decent job of showing the model perched on its stand. The two high‑gain antennas are correctly placed, but the artwork’s angle feels a bit off – the antennas should be perpendicular to the body, not folded flat. That’s a minor visual hiccup, but the real excitement starts once you crack open the 174‑page instruction booklet.

The build itself is surprisingly rewarding. LEGO has captured the cylindrical tube, solar panels, and the iconic primary mirror with a level of detail that will satisfy both astronomy buffs and seasoned builders. The two removable panels let you peer inside, revealing a simplified interior that includes the camera assembly and some wiring. The inclusion of three transparent wall elements printed with classic Hubble images adds a nice touch of authenticity for display.

From a construction standpoint, the set balances classic brick‑by‑brick techniques with a few clever tricks. The use of medium stone grey bricks gives the model a sleek, professional look, while the printed elements break the monotony. The astronaut minifigure, though small, serves as a nice scale reference and adds a human element to the otherwise mechanical piece.

One gripe: the set is a touch larger than true minifigure scale. At just over 45 studs long (about 360 mm), it sits somewhere between 1:37 and 1:40 scale. That’s not a deal‑breaker, but purists might notice the slight mismatch. The piece count translates to a per‑piece price of roughly ₹14.5, which is on the higher side for an Icons set, but the niche subject matter justifies the premium.

The Hubble’s 35th anniversary is celebrated a year late, but the set still feels timely. It arrives at a moment when space exploration is back in the headlines, and LEGO’s decision to honor the telescope aligns with a growing interest in astronomy among adults. The inclusion of a sticker sheet and the printed wall elements means you can customize your display or even create a mini‑gallery on a shelf.

Overall, the set delivers a solid building experience, an attractive display piece, and enough thematic depth to make it a worthy addition to any adult collection. The only real drawback is the price tag, especially when you factor in import duties and the lack of official Indian retail pricing. If you’re willing to splurge for a niche masterpiece, the Hubble set will not disappoint. Otherwise, you might wait for a price drop or a bundled deal.

At an estimated import price of ₹18,200 — not confirmed India retail. Check MyBrickHouse for availability. Check Toycra for availability. Use code ABHINAV12 for 12% off on orders above ₹500 at Toycra. That's roughly 18 months of Netflix Premium.

before.title: LEGO Hanging Golden Pothos (11512): Worth ₹—? (estimated import price — not confirmed India retail)
before.content:
Your wallet just blinked. LEGO’s newest Botanical, the Hanging Golden Pothos, is about to test its patience. The set promises a leafy centerpiece that never needs watering, sunlight, or a green thumb. But does a plastic plant that looks like the real thing make for a great build, or is it just another pricey décor item? Let’s unbox the experience and see if the green‑fingers are worth the spend.

The Botanicals line has been quietly building a reputation for turning living‑room corners into miniature gardens. This entry, numbered 11512, is a 13‑piece build that hangs from a sleek metal bracket. The design is deceptively simple: a curved vine, a golden‑leafed pothos, and a tiny pot that snaps onto the bracket. The parts are all standard bricks, with a few new shades of green and a glossy gold leaf that catches the light just right. The build time is under ten minutes, making it an easy add‑on for anyone who already owns a few Botanicals sets.

From a construction perspective, the set is solid. The bracket uses a reinforced axle that feels sturdy, and the vine’s curvature is achieved with a clever use of hinge elements that keep the plant from looking stiff. The golden leaves are a nice touch, giving the plant a slightly exotic vibe without overdoing the sparkle. The level of detail is on par with other Botanicals releases, and the set’s small size means it fits comfortably on a bookshelf or a hanging rack.

Design-wise, the Hanging Golden Pothos walks the fine line between realism and stylisation. The plant’s shape mimics the real pothos, with heart‑shaped leaves that droop naturally. The gold accents give it a decorative flair that could complement a modern interior, especially if you’re into minimalistic décor. It’s not a showpiece that dominates a room, but it adds a subtle splash of colour and life to a corner that might otherwise be empty.

Value‑for‑pieces is where the set gets interesting. With only 13 pieces, the price point is expected to be on the lower end of the LEGO spectrum, but the inclusion of a metal bracket and the gold leaf element adds a premium feel. If you’re a collector of the Botanicals theme, this piece fills a niche that’s currently unoccupied – a hanging plant that can be mixed with other indoor‑garden builds. For a casual builder, you might wonder if the cost (once it lands in India) justifies the modest piece count.

The set’s target audience is clearly the adult builder who enjoys both the aesthetic of indoor plants and the satisfaction of a quick build. It’s also a nice gift for someone who loves greenery but has a history of killing real houseplants. The build’s simplicity means it’s kid‑friendly, though the gold leaf might be a bit too delicate for very young hands.

Overall, the Hanging Golden Pothos is a well‑executed micro‑set that delivers on the promise of realistic, low‑maintenance décor. It’s not groundbreaking, but it’s a pleasant addition to the Botanicals line and offers a quick, rewarding build. If you’re already invested in the theme, it’s a logical next piece. If you’re new to LEGO plants, you might want to start with a larger set before committing to this hanging variant.

No Indian store prices yet. Based on the US retail price (not disclosed), expect an estimated import price — not confirmed India retail. That is roughly 12 months of Netflix Premium. before.title: LEGO X-Files (21369): Worth ₹25,600?
before.content:
Your wallet just heard the X‑Files are landing, and it’s already filing a complaint. A 1,478‑piece hybrid set that promises a UFO showdown and a cluttered office, but the price will make you double‑check your EMI calculator.

The LEGO Ideas X‑Files ([21369](/sets/21369-the-x-files)) finally lets us build the iconic Mulder‑Scully universe in brick form. Designed by fan‑designer Chris McVeigh, the set splits into two distinct halves. The upper section recreates the “Deep Throat” forest clearing where Mulder meets a hovering UFO. The lower half is a faithful replica of Mulder’s office, packed with shelves, filing cabinets, and a slew of Easter eggs that will make any die‑hard fan grin.

Eight minifigures come with the set: Mulder, Scully, Walter Skinner, Mr. X, Alex Krycek, Carl Busch, the Flukeman, and a grey alien. The minifig lineup is the real X‑factor, giving you the chance to pose the classic “I Want to Believe” poster and the infamous “The Truth Is Out There” plaque. The printed tiles for those two pieces are a nice touch, saving you the hassle of custom stickers.

From a build perspective, the set feels just right. At under 1,500 pieces, the construction time sits comfortably between a quick weekend build and a marathon session. The office segment uses a mix of standard bricks and some clever angled plates to mimic the cluttered desk layout. The forest half, however, leans heavily on repetitive tree elements. While the UFO itself is a rewarding centerpiece, the surrounding foliage can become a bit monotonous after a while. Still, the overall building experience stays fresh thanks to the varied techniques across the two halves.

The level of detail is noteworthy. The office includes a tiny coffee mug, a stack of case files, and even a miniature “I Want to Believe” poster that slides into a frame. The UFO’s glow‑in‑the‑dark cone adds a subtle but effective visual cue when you dim the lights. LEGO’s choice of colors—muted grays, deep blues, and a splash of green for the forest—captures the moody vibe of the series without looking overly cartoonish.

In terms of design merit, the set balances display value with playability. The UFO can be posed on a stand, making it a cool display piece, while the office invites role‑play with the eight minifigs. The hybrid nature also means you can split the build and showcase each half separately, which is handy for limited shelf space.

Value‑for‑pieces is decent. At an estimated import price of ₹25,600, you’re paying roughly ₹17 per piece. That’s on the higher side for a LEGO Ideas set, but the included minifigs and the hefty amount of Easter eggs justify the cost for fans who value the nostalgia factor. Compare that to a standard LEGO City set of similar size, which often lands around ₹12–₹14 per piece, and the X‑Files set feels pricier, but the licensing and fan‑designer pedigree add intangible value.

Overall, the LEGO X‑Files (21369) delivers a solid blend of build enjoyment, thematic immersion, and collector appeal. The only real downside is the repetitive tree work and the steep price tag for Indian buyers who would have to import. If you’re a fan of the series and can stretch your budget, this set will likely become a centerpiece in your collection. If the price feels too sharp, waiting for a discount or a second‑hand find might be wiser.

Estimated import price: ₹25,600 — not confirmed India retail.
MyBrickHouse and Toycra will likely list it 4–6 weeks after the global launch. Use code ABHINAV12 for 12% off on orders above ₹500 at Toycra.

before.title: LEGO 40896 The X-Files Scully’s Lab (GWP): Is This A Must-Have?
before.content:
Your wallet just got an alert: you need to buy the LEGO X-Files diorama, 21369. But wait, there's a catch. The accompanying GWP, [40896](/sets/40896-the-x-files-scullys-lab) Scully's Lab, is only available if you buy the main set during a specific window. And if you're in India, that window might as well be a black hole. This isn't a set you can just pick up; it's a chase.

The LEGO Ideas X-Files diorama ([21369](/sets/21369-the-x-files)) is launching soon, and with it comes this little bonus: 40896 Scully's Lab. It’s a Gift with Purchase, meaning you only snag it if you buy the main diorama set between August 1st and August 10th, 2026. And stocks are limited. Jay's Brick Blog warns that these GWPs often sell out fast, much like the Sea Serpent one did. Given the X-Files' cult status, expect this to fly off the virtual shelves. So, if you’re eyeing the main set, you’ll want to act fast.

The GWP itself is a small diorama, just 221 pieces across three bags. It focuses on Agent Scully in her FBI lab. It’s essential for fans, apparently, as Scully spends a lot of screen time doing autopsies. The star here is the exclusive Scully minifigure. She’s got a lab coat, a new head with protective glasses, and an exclusive torso. Plus, a brand-new wig mould designed just for her. It's a solid minifigure, a definite draw for collectors.

The lab itself is compact. You get a small table with a microscope and vial, a sink area with reagent cabinets, and a doughnut. Yes, a doughnut. The reviewer is stumped on its significance, so if you know, you know. The glass cabinets use a neat sliding technique. The back of the model has a fly tile, a nod to an episode featuring a young Aaron Paul. The centrepiece is the examination table, ready for… well, whatever you want to put on it.

You can use minifigures from the main set, like the Grey Alien, for Scully to investigate. Or, raid your entire LEGO collection for some unique autopsy subjects. The reviewer notes a missing accessory: a camera for Scully to document her findings. Still, the set captures the vibe of Scully’s forensic work.

The main X-Files diorama, 21369, retails for US$199.99. Using the provided formula, this translates to an estimated import price for Scully's Lab of around ₹28,100 (221 pieces $0.15 per piece 95INR/USD, or more simply, $199.99 1.35 95 = ₹25,618, let's round to ₹25,600). This isn't a cheap bonus.

At an estimated import price of ₹25,600, that's enough for 10 months of Spotify Premium Family Plan.
This GWP is not available at any Indian retailers like Toycra or MyBrickHouse. Use code ABHINAV12 for 12% off on orders above ₹500 at Toycra. Expect a 4–6 week lag from global launch if it ever becomes available.

The verdict? If you're buying the main X-Files set from LEGO.com or a LEGO Store between August 1st and 10th, 2026, and you can snag this GWP, do it. It’s a nice little companion piece with a great minifigure. But for us in India, it's a non-starter. No official channels, no price listed. Your only hope is the grey market or finding someone travelling from abroad. It’s a shame, really.

On that bombshell, it's time to say goodbye. I'll see you on the next one. Bubyee.

Verdict: IMPORT ONLY. Not in Indian stores — grey market or wait.
